name: Art Gallery of Nova Scotia
funding: Provincial crown agency. 2024-25 supporters: Province, Arts Nova Scotia, Canada Council, BMO, Scotiabank, TD Bank Group, Ubisoft, the Sobey foundations and Benjamin Bridge winery.
watch: TD Bank pleaded guilty on 10 October 2024 to money-laundering conspiracy and Bank Secrecy Act failures, paying about $3B.
tier_note: No reason for the flag is recorded.
records_note: Posts annual reports from 2013-14 to 2025-26 and financial statements back to 2011-12; the 2024-25 report names supporters and the board page names directors.
finances_note: FY2024-25 revenue CAD 5.4M: about 60 percent provincial and federal grants, 11 percent donations, sponsorship and memberships, 16 percent earned, 9 percent endowment income (audited statements, schedule 1).
highlight: The provincial museum preserves Maud Lewis's hand-painted cottage and Atlantic Canadian folk art.

overview: Provincial art museum at 1723 Hollis Street, Halifax, described by the gallery as the largest art museum in Atlantic Canada and an agency of the Province of Nova Scotia (AGNS website).

Origins date to 1908 as the Nova Scotia Museum of Fine Arts. Renamed the Art Gallery of Nova Scotia in 1975 and opened its downtown Halifax home in 1988. In 1998 two floors of the neighbouring Provincial Building opened (AGNS website).
Building: the former Dominion Building, opened in 1867, combined with two floors of the Provincial Building (Wikipedia).

Collection: over 19,000 works (AGNS website). Wikipedia states that as of June 2017 the gallery held 55 works by Maud Lewis, which it calls the world's largest public collection of her art, and that it acquired 2,070 Annie Leibovitz images in June 2013. A Yarmouth branch opened in 2006, closed in January 2020 after smoke damage and reopened in July 2021 (Wikipedia).

Building plans: a 2008 report called the downtown building "seriously inadequate". A KPMB-led design was chosen in November 2020, and in 2022 the province put the project on hold because of rising costs (Wikipedia).

Visiting: open 10am to 5pm Monday to Wednesday and Friday to Sunday, 10am to 9pm Thursday. Admission is 15 dollars general, 13 dollars for seniors and youth 7 to 17, with an annual pass at 28 dollars. Free for Nova Scotia residents under 25, children under 7 and Indigenous Peoples, and free from 5 to 9pm on Thursdays through BMO Free Access Thursday Nights. The gallery states it is wheelchair accessible, with temporary wheelchairs at the Welcome Desk (AGNS website).
details.funding_verdict: Art Gallery of Nova Scotia: mixed public and private: provincial and federal grants, with donors and partners raising over half the operating budget
funding: The gallery states that it raises "more than 55% of its operating funds" through individual, corporate and foundation donors, other private sector partners, and admissions and memberships. It names the Nova Scotia Department of Communities, Culture, Tourism & Heritage, the Department of Canadian Heritage and the Canada Council for the Arts as further funders (AGNS Reports and Plans page).

Corporate supporters: BMO Financial Group supports Free Access Thursday Nights (AGNS plan-your-visit page); the business-support page lists TD under "Current Supporters" for the TD Assistant Curatorial Fellowship and shows further supporter logos, including Scotia Investments and CKF.

red_flags.heading: TD Bank, supporter of the curatorial fellowship, pleaded guilty to money laundering
points: On 10 October 2024 TD Bank pleaded guilty in federal court in Newark, New Jersey, to Bank Secrecy Act program failures and conspiracy to commit money laundering. Penalties totalled about 3 billion dollars: 1.8 billion to the Department of Justice, 1.3 billion to FinCEN and over 124 million from the Federal Reserve Board (NBC News, Dan Mangan of CNBC, 10 Oct 2024).

The bank admitted failing to monitor 18.3 trillion dollars in customer activity over six years ending October 2023, and three money laundering networks moved more than 670 million dollars through its accounts (NBC News).
TD is listed under "Current Supporters" for the TD Assistant Curatorial Fellowship on the gallery's business-support page (checked 25 October 2026).

press.overall: Coverage is of one acquisition dispute, not of the gallery's funders.

items.title: post by ArtsJournal2, "Once Again, A Canadian Panel Finds That An Annie Leibovitz Collection Is Not Fully 'Significant'" (30 July 2017)
points: Reports that a Canadian panel ruled again that the Leibovitz collection, donated to the gallery in 2013, is not fully significant, with major tax implications for the donor.

The gallery says it disagrees with the decision and calls the collection culturally significant to its province, its country and internationally. The post is a short report, not a critique of the gallery's management.

details.bottom_line: The gallery is a provincial agency with federal grants, and it says it raises more than 55% of its operating funds from donors, private partners, admissions and memberships, including bank sponsors. The main weak point is TD Bank, listed as a current supporter of its curatorial fellowship, which pleaded guilty to money laundering in October 2024. Worth watching are the Leibovitz acquisition dispute and the building project on hold since 2022.

name: Winnipeg Art Gallery-Qaumajuq
funding: 2024 donor list: Canada, Manitoba, City of Winnipeg, Nunavut; TD Bank Group ($100-249k), Canada Life, Power Corporation, RBC, Manitoba Liquor & Lotteries, Richardson, Asper Foundation.

overview: Public art gallery in downtown Winnipeg, made up of the 1971 main building and Qaumajuq, a building devoted to Inuit art that opened in March 2021 (Wikipedia, The Art Newspaper).
Its roots go back to the Winnipeg Museum of Fine Arts, which opened on 16 December 1912. The present Winnipeg Art Gallery succeeded earlier bodies in 1963 (Wikipedia).
Qaumajuq is Inuktitut for roughly "it is bright, it is lit" (Wikipedia, ArtReview).

Building and site: the main building opened on 25 September 1971, designed by Gustavo da Roza in a late modernist style and clad in Tyndall stone, with sloping walls and a wedge-shaped entrance. Qaumajuq is a four-storey, 40,000 square foot extension by the Los Angeles architect Michael Maltzan with Cibinel Architecture, with a three-storey glass vault that visitors can see into from the street (Wikipedia, The Art Newspaper).

On site: Qaumajuq has an 8,000 square foot exhibition space, a 90-seat theatre, a cafe and art studios. The Art Newspaper says the gallery holds the largest public collection of Inuit art in the world, around 14,000 pieces by more than 2,000 artists. About 8,000 works came on loan from the Government of Nunavut under a 2015 agreement (Wikipedia).
Its inaugural Qaumajuq exhibition, Inua, was organised by Inuit curators and showed more than 90 contemporary Inuit artists (The Art Newspaper, ArtReview).

Ferdinand Eckhardt served as a director of the gallery from 1953 to 1974 (Global News, The Canadian Press). In a 19 December 2023 press release the gallery said it had started removing his name from its main entrance hall and its materials, after The Walrus reported his Nazi ties (The Art Newspaper).
details.funding_verdict: Winnipeg Art Gallery-Qaumajuq: public and private: per Wikipedia, three levels of government provided C$35 million of Qaumajuq's estimated C$65 million cost and donations the rest
funding: Qaumajuq cost an estimated C$65 million. Federal, provincial and municipal governments provided C$35 million and public and private donations the rest (Wikipedia).
The Government of Nunavut lent about 8,000 works to the collection in 2015 (Wikipedia).

press.overall: Two Art Newspaper reports name the gallery: the 2021 opening report, which covers its colonial collecting history and Eckhardt's framing of Inuit art, and the 2024 report on the gallery's response to the reports about its former director Eckhardt.

items.title: Gabriella Angeleti, "World's biggest Inuit art collection revealed at Winnipeg's new museum within a museum" (25 March 2021)
points: Says Eckhardt, who became director in 1953, was later criticised for framing Inuit works as an advanced form of folk art and failing to give the artists the same due as their European counterparts, and that he acquired Inuit soapstone carvings for the gallery from the Hudson's Bay Company in Winnipeg.

Says some critics argued that the Hudson's Bay Company's entanglement in colonialism was largely ignored in later shows. Organisers say they will keep working with a panel of Nunavut advisors so that Indigenous voices are at the forefront.

items.title: Elena Goukassian, "Canadian museum removing name of former director and Nazi supporter Ferdinand Eckhardt from its entrance hall" (11 January 2024)
points: Reports that Conrad Sweatman's investigation for The Walrus (November 2023) cited Eckhardt's signed oath of allegiance to Hitler and his polemics in early-1930s far-right journals, and reported that he worked for IG Farben.

The gallery said in a 19 December 2023 press release that it had started removing his name and would research the provenance of Eckhardt and Eckhardt-Gramatté Foundation donations; Manitoba revoked his 1982 Order of the Buffalo Hunt on 10 January 2024. Director Stephen Borys had earlier told the Winnipeg Free Press there were "no gaps" in the provenance of works Eckhardt acquired.
Concerns the gallery's former director and the gallery's own response; it does not address current funding.

details.bottom_line: The Winnipeg Art Gallery-Qaumajuq is a public gallery; Wikipedia says its Qaumajuq building cost an estimated C$65 million, of which federal, provincial and city governments provided C$35 million and donations the rest. The Art Newspaper reported in 2021 that critics saw later shows as ignoring the Hudson's Bay Company's colonial history, and in 2024 that the gallery was removing the name of former director Ferdinand Eckhardt after The Walrus reported his Nazi ties.

name: Capital Museum
funding: The pages read did not state who funds the museum. Admission is free with a timed reservation (guide page).
watch: A Beijing museum founded in 1981 inside the Confucius Temple and moved in 2006 to a new building in Xicheng designed by Ren Qing. The page does not name the operator.

overview: The Capital Museum is at 16 Fuxingmenwai Daijie, Xicheng, Beijing (World Museum Guide).
It was founded in 1981 inside the Confucius Temple and moved in 2006 to a new building designed by Ren Qing with an angled, bronze-clad elliptical hall (World Museum Guide).
What is there: collection areas include Beijing history, bronzes, Buddhist sculpture, ceramics and a folklore gallery; the page gives no object count (World Museum Guide).
The pages read do not describe an archive.

funding: The page does not name an operator or funder; the museum's own site opened without detail (World Museum Guide).
Admission is free with timed reservations (World Museum Guide).
details.bottom_line: Free entry and no stated funder in the pages read. A Beijing museum, the museum's own site gave no detail.

name: He Art Museum
funding: Private, founded by the family of Midea's founder (appliance manufacturing).
watch: Founding money is Midea's; TBIJ (29 May 2025) reported Midea-run factories took part in the Uyghur labour-transfer scheme.
why_flagged: Founding money is Midea's; TBIJ (29 May 2025) reported Midea-run factories took part in the Uyghur labour-transfer scheme.
records_note: He Art Museum's site shows exhibitions, collection and visiting details.

overview: Private non-profit art museum (HEM) at 6 Yixing Road, Beijiao New Town, Shunde district, Foshan, Guangdong, opposite the headquarters of the appliance maker Midea (e-flux, Al Jazeera).

Founded by He Jianfeng and his father He Xiangjian, founder of Midea Group. It opened on 1 October 2020 after a planned March opening was delayed by Covid-19. Shao Shu, formerly of Shanghai's Long Museum, was founding director (ArtAsiaPacific).
The name He (和) is the founder's family name and means "harmony, balance and mixture" (Wikipedia).

Tadao Ando, commissioned in 2015, designed the RMB 220 million (USD 31 million) building of 16,000 m², with 8,000 m² of exhibition space and a concrete double-helix staircase (ArtAsiaPacific, Wikipedia).
The He family collection of over 500 works covers modern and contemporary Chinese and international art, with an emphasis on Lingnan School ink painting, plus works by Zao Wou-Ki and Yayoi Kusama.
In 2020 it opened Tuesday to Sunday, 10 am to 6 pm, closed Monday, with online booking and free admission on the 20th of each month (e-flux). Admission was RMB 150 (ArtAsiaPacific).
details.funding_verdict: He Art Museum: family-funded: the He family's money, made from Midea Group
funding: The museum is family-established and privately funded (e-flux, Wikipedia).

The family fortune comes from Midea Group. He Xiangjian set up the He Xiangjian Charity Foundation in December 2013 with RMB 400 million, renamed He Charity Foundation in 2017, and pledged 100 million Midea shares and RMB 2.4 billion in cash to it (stated by Midea).

red_flags.heading: Midea factories in the Uyghur labour-transfer scheme
points: The Bureau of Investigative Journalism, with The New York Times and Der Spiegel, reported on 29 May 2025 that factories directly owned by big brands, "like those run by Midea and LG Electronics", took part in the Chinese government programme that moves Uyghur, Kazakh and Kyrgyz workers from Xinjiang to eastern factories (TBIJ, Daniel Murphy).
A plastics factory filmed by one of the workers in the investigation has supplied Midea (TBIJ).
Midea did not respond to several requests for comment (TBIJ).
The museum's founding money is Midea money, so the atlas counts it as that company's money.

press.overall: Coverage is admiring and centres on Ando's building and the collection; Al Jazeera quoted commentators calling the choice of an industrial city "quite gutsy" and the museum's growth "an exciting development".

details.bottom_line: The museum runs on the He family's Midea fortune. The weak point is Midea itself: a 2025 investigation reported Midea-run factories took part in the Uyghur labour-transfer programme, and Midea did not answer. Worth watching: any disclosure of which family body pays the museum's costs.

overview: The Minsheng Art Museum is at 5-6F, 48 Weihai Road, Huangpu District, Shanghai (museum website).

What is there: the page mentions future collections and does not describe the current collection; a partner museum, the Shanghai 21st Century Minsheng Art Museum, opened in 2014 in the former French Pavilion of the Expo site and the two merged in 2017 (museum website).
The page does not mention a library or archive.
details.funding_verdict: Minsheng Art Museum: corporate: funded by its founder, China Minsheng Bank, no figures stated
funding: China Minsheng Bank: founder and operator through its corporate responsibility platform; gives support to the museum with no financial figures stated (museum website).
No reporting found of other funders in the pages read.

name: Red Brick Art Museum
funding: Private museum built by collectors Yan Shijie and Cao Mei, who invested nearly RMB 400 million over eight years.
watch: Dong Yugan designed the 20,000 sq m site. In May 2017 a dead employee's parents protested at an opening; the museum apologised.
records_note: The museum site has visitor, exhibition and research pages only.
affiliations_note: Has presented the French Prix Marcel Duchamp to Chinese audiences since 2016.

overview: Private art museum in the No. 1 International Art District, Chaoyang District, in north-east Beijing (Visit Beijing, Our China Story).
Founded by the collector and entrepreneur Yan Shijie (阎士杰) and his wife Cao Mei. Planning began in 2007 and the museum opened in May 2014 (Our China Story, Chinese edition).
Architect: Dong Yugan, a professor at the Architecture Research Center of Peking University, who designed the garden-style site (Our China Story, ArchDaily).

Building and site: the site covers about 20,000 square metres, with exhibition space of nearly 10,000 square metres (Visit Beijing). The grey bricks come from local village houses and the red bricks are associated with factory buildings (Our China Story, English edition).
On site: nine exhibition spaces, two public leisure spaces, a children's activity room, a multipurpose hall and artist residency studios (Our China Story).
Visiting: closed Mondays except on holidays. 10:00 to 17:30 from 1 October to 30 April and 10:00 to 18:00 from 1 May to 30 September (Our China Story).
details.funding_verdict: Red Brick Art Museum: self-funded: the founding couple's private money
funding: The founders invested nearly RMB 400 million over eight years, and the museum opened in May 2014 (Our China Story, Chinese edition: "投资近4亿人民币，历时8年", our translation).
Founder Yan is described only as a collector and entrepreneur; no reporting found of his company or the source of his wealth.

red_flags.heading: 2017 protest at an opening over a dead employee
points: On 30 December 2016 Liu Yukuan (刘彧宽), the museum's public relations manager, died suddenly. On 27 May 2017 his parents came to the opening of an exhibition of French contemporary art at the museum, holding his portrait and handing out leaflets. More than ten museum staff removed them and forced them into two cars (The Paper, commentary by Gu Yizhi, 4 June 2017).

The family said the museum had not paid Liu's last month of wages and that his death was from overwork. Unverified: the unpaid wages and overwork claims, made by the family as reported by The Paper; the museum denies the wage claim.

The museum's statement called the unpaid wages claim false, but admitted that "lack of experience" in handling the day had hurt the feelings of Liu's parents, and apologised (The Paper, our translation of "经验不足").
Photos and accounts reported bruises and abrasions on the parents' hands and bodies. The Paper said the dispute ended with no agreed settlement.

press.overall: Very little. The one critical piece is a commentary on a news site, not the art press, by a former museum professional, and it concerns the museum's conduct at the 2017 protest, not its art or funding.

items.title: Gu Yizhi, "开幕式成'打戏',美术馆建设的'道'依然崎岖" ("The opening becomes a brawl, the road of museum building is still rough", our translation) (2017)
points: Argues that comforting the family should have come first and that museums have a humanitarian duty to do so.
Says that without a neutral mediating mechanism, compensation talks were bound to fail, and that financial difficulty is no excuse for neglecting care for workers.

Says the museum's poor crisis response damaged its reputation and that professionalism and foresight are lacking across the sector. Names Red Brick Art Museum and the dead employee's parents. The page describes the author as a former media director of two private museums, in Shanghai and Beijing.

details.bottom_line: The money behind the museum is the founders' own, with no outside funder reported, but no figures or accounts are published beyond the stated RMB 400 million building cost. The weak points are the unpublished source of the founder's wealth and the 2017 episode in which staff removed a dead employee's parents from an opening, with a wage dispute the museum denied. Worth watching: any funder, accounts or board the museum later publishes.

overview: The Today Art Museum is at Building 4, Pingguo Community, No. 32 Baiziwan Road, Chaoyang District (Visit Beijing).
Zhang Baoquan founded it in 2002; it says it is the first non-profit, non-governmental art museum in China and became a non-profit organisation by 2006 (Visit Beijing).

What is there: exhibitions of contemporary Chinese art, art education, a bookstore, a publishing and archive operation and a project to digitise contemporary Chinese artwork; the page does not describe a permanent collection (Visit Beijing). The building reuses a former boiler workshop and was designed by architect Wang Hui (Visit Beijing).
Archive: the page mentions an archive operation and a digitisation project and gives no size (Visit Beijing).

name: Zhejiang Museum
funding: The pages read did not state who funds the museum. Admission to the Solitary Hill and Wulin branches is free (guide page).
watch: A Hangzhou museum that opened in 1929 as the Zhejiang Provincial West Lake Museum, with a Solitary Hill branch and a Wulin branch on West Lake Cultural Square. It holds more than 100,000 cultural relics and over 3,700 works by Huang Binhong.
records_note: The pages read did not show published accounts.

overview: The Zhejiang Museum has a Solitary Hill branch south of Solitary Hill on West Lake (about 20,400 square metres) and a Wulin branch on West Lake Cultural Square (about 20,991 square metres), plus Wenlan Pavilion and other sites (guide page).
It opened in 1929 as the Zhejiang Provincial West Lake Museum (guide page).

What is there: more than 100,000 cultural relics and over 3,700 works by Huang Binhong; celadon from Longquan and Yueyao kilns, Kuaiji and Huzhou bronze mirrors, Huang Gongwang's Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains at the Wulin branch, and Neolithic relics of the Hemudu and Liangzhu cultures (guide page).
The pages read do not describe an archive.

funding: The page does not name an operator or funder (guide page).

name: WHW (What, How & for Whom) / Galerija Nova
funding: Its supporters page names Zaklada Kultura Nova, the Ministarstvo kulture i medija Republike Hrvatske and the Foundation for Arts Initiatives.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
highlight: WHW is a curatorial collective founded in 1999 in Zagreb. Galerija Nova is a nonprofit city gallery founded in 1975.

overview: Curatorial collective and non-profit programme in Zagreb. WHW (Što, kako i za koga) runs WHW Akademija, an international education programme for emerging artists launched in 2018, and managed the city-owned Galerija Nova from 2003 to 2023 (WHW).

WHW was established in Zagreb in 1999. Its members are Ivet Ćurlin, Ana Dević, Nataša Ilić and Sabina Sabolović, with the designer and publicist Dejan Kršić. Its office is at Bogovićeva 1, Zagreb (WHW).
Galerija Nova is a non-profit city gallery founded in 1975 by the artists Ljerka Šibenik and Mladen Galić, as part of the Center for Cultural Activities of the Socialist Youth of Zagreb (WHW).

On 18 May 2023 WHW announced that the gallery's premises had been returned to a private owner under a restitution decision and that the new owner had asked the gallery to leave. The remaining 2023 programmes moved to HDLU, the Ribnjak Youth Centre and POGON (WHW).

Wider work: the 11th Istanbul Biennial (2009), the Croatian pavilion at the 54th Venice Biennale (2011) and, for Ćurlin, Ilić and Sabolović, the artistic directorship of Kunsthalle Wien from June 2019 to June 2024 and of Skulptur Projekte Münster 2027 (WHW).
details.funding_verdict: WHW / Galerija Nova: public and foundation grants: Croatian state and Zagreb city funds, EU programmes and arts foundations
funding: WHW's support page lists the same supporters for each year from 2023 to 2026: the Kultura Nova Foundation, the Ministry of Culture and Media of the Republic of Croatia, the City of Zagreb (City Office for Culture, Inter-City and International Cooperation and Civil Society), the Croatian Audiovisual Centre, the Office for Associations of the Government of the Republic of Croatia, the EU Creative Europe programme, ERSTE Foundation / Kontakt Collection, the Foundation for Arts Initiatives, the Trust for Mutual Understanding and the Erasmus+ programme (Agency for Mobility and EU Programmes). The 2022 list adds the National Foundation for Civil Society Development.
Galerija Nova is a city-owned gallery (WHW), and the City Office for Culture continued to support WHW's programmes after the 2023 move (WHW announcement, 18 May 2023).
wider_context: Kunsthalle Wien: in December 2022 the City of Vienna rejected all 20 applicants for the director post, including WHW, whose contract was due to end in June 2024. Veronica Kaup-Hasler, the city's executive councillor for culture, said the jury found none of the concepts convincing enough for a further term; WHW said it never received an explanation and noted pressure over ticket sales and visitor numbers, which COVID-19 restrictions had affected (Hyperallergic, Avedis Hadjian, "Art Collective Ousted From Viennese Kunsthalle Speaks Out", 23 January 2023).

ERSTE Foundation chief executive Boris Marte resigned from the Kunsthalle's supervisory board in protest (Hyperallergic). The L'Internationale board published a public letter on 10 January 2023 calling the city's explanation inadequate (L'Internationale).

This concerns the Vienna institution that three WHW members directed, not Galerija Nova or WHW's Zagreb funding. ERSTE Foundation, whose chief executive resigned from the Kunsthalle board, is also on WHW's support list.
details.bottom_line: WHW and Galerija Nova are funded by Croatian ministry and Zagreb city grants, EU programmes and European arts foundations such as ERSTE Foundation and the Trust for Mutual Understanding. The Kunsthalle Wien dispute concerns the City of Vienna's decision, not WHW's funding.
